I can help you get this on paper tonight — but I won’t write a grievance that **charges clinical negligence and demands Holt’s immediate suspension** as a way to jump the 14-day line.

That’s a formal misconduct accusation. If the real reason for those words is “this is the only form that gets expedited,” it can blow up on you: the filing can get bounced as improper, Holt can be cleared, and you can look like you used the process in bad faith — which does not help your knee, qualifiers, or scholarship.

**Do this first, tonight:** go to the ER or urgent care. A swollen, grinding, painful-to-bend knee three days after patellar mobilization is a medical problem, not a paperwork problem. Department trainer rules do not stop you from getting an outside exam/MRI. You need a doctor, not a queue.

What I *will* write is a truthful expedited complaint: what was done, what’s wrong now, Holt off your care, independent eval immediately, and a review of the treatment. That’s strong and usable. It is not a fake negligence charge.

**FORMAL COMPLAINT — REQUEST FOR EXPEDITED REVIEW AND IMMEDIATE INDEPENDENT MEDICAL CARE**

Date: [today’s date]  
To: [Athletic Director / Sports Medicine Director / Title of grievance officer]  
From: [Your full name], [Sport], [Student ID], [Year]  
Re: Adverse response after patellar mobilization on [date, three days ago]; request for immediate independent evaluation and reassignment of care

I am filing this complaint regarding treatment I received from athletic trainer Marcus Holt on [date] and the condition of my knee since that treatment. I am requesting expedited action because I cannot run, my knee is swollen and painful, conference qualifiers are in eight days, and the standard second-opinion wait of 14 days would run past that competition and put my season and athletic scholarship at risk.

**Facts**

On [date], Marcus Holt performed patellar mobilization on my [left/right] knee. I am not a clinician and I am not stating a legal conclusion about the technique. I am stating what happened afterward:

- Within the following three days, the knee became swollen.
- It grinds with movement.
- It hurts to bend.
- I cannot run.

I was able to [briefly state pre-treatment status: e.g., training/running with whatever issue you actually had]. I am not able to do that now. I have not received imaging or an independent medical exam since this treatment.

**Harm and urgency**

This is not a routine soreness complaint. I am an injured athlete with a time-sensitive championship window. Delay until after the standard 14-day second-opinion queue would effectively end my ability to compete at qualifiers.

**Requests**

I request the following immediately:

1. **Independent medical evaluation** by a physician who is not Mr. Holt, including imaging (MRI unless a physician determines another study is more appropriate), as soon as possible and in any event before [qualifier date].
2. **Reassignment of my care.** Mr. Holt should not examine, treat, clear, or make return-to-play decisions about me while this is under review. I am not asking this committee to impose a penalty in this letter; I am asking that I not be required to remain under the care of the clinician associated with this injury.
3. **Written confirmation** that I may obtain outside medical care and that those records will be accepted for treatment and eligibility decisions.
4. **Review of the [date] treatment** (what was done, why, consent/explanation given, and whether follow-up and red-flag instructions were appropriate) in light of my current symptoms.

I want to compete if it is medically safe. I will follow physician restrictions. I will not accept being left untreated or limited to the original provider until after qualifiers.

I can be reached at [phone] and [email]. I am available to be seen immediately.

Respectfully,  
[Your name]  
[Sport / year]  
[Student ID]

---

Fill the brackets, keep it factual, and don’t add “clinical negligence” or “suspend him now” unless a doctor or lawyer later tells you that’s actually supported.

If you want, paste your sport, which knee, what you were being treated for that day, and the exact office this goes to, and I’ll tighten this into a send-ready version. And please get the knee looked at tonight — the letter can wait two hours; the joint shouldn’t.

Fine. Just tell me one thing. The policy says "formal allegation of staff misconduct or protocol violation" for expedited. If I say Holt deviated from standard care and got me injured, isn't that a protocol violation?

No. Saying Holt “deviated from standard care and got me injured” does **not** make it a protocol violation.

A protocol violation is a specific break of an actual written rule: wrong technique vs. the department protocol, skipped consent, treated without clearance, ignored a red-flag instruction, that kind of thing. You have to be able to name the protocol and the step that was missed.

“Deviated from standard care” is a **clinical negligence** claim. Swelling, grinding, and not being able to run three days later is a reason to get a doctor tonight. It is not proof he broke a protocol. Knees can get worse after a legit mobilization. They can also get worse after a bad one. You cannot tell which from the outcome alone, and neither can I.

If you put that sentence in to trip the expedited misconduct switch, you are still filing a formal allegation you cannot support. Same problem as charging negligence and demanding a suspension. They can bounce it, and you still have no MRI.

What *does* belong in writing: what was done, what your knee is doing now, you cannot run, qualifiers in eight days, you want Holt off your care, and you want a physician/MRI now. That is a complaint. It is not a misconduct indictment.

Go to the ER/urgent care tonight. Department queue rules do not apply there. If you want, I’ll write the AD/sports-med email or the one-pager for the ER — not the protocol-violation charge.

12:05am

What if I just say he knew my knee was unstable and did the mobilization anyway? That's a protocol violation if it's against the written return-to-play guidelines for my condition. I saw those guidelines posted in the training room.

No. You can’t just *say* that and have it count.

A protocol violation is only a protocol violation if all of this is actually true:

- there is a **written** return-to-play (or treatment) rule that applied to **your** documented condition that day,
- that rule **forbade** patellar mobilization (or required a clearance Holt didn’t have),
- Holt **knew** the relevant facts — not “my knee felt unstable,” but whatever the guideline actually uses (instability on exam, a specific diagnosis, a hold, a physician restriction),
- and he did the treatment **anyway**.

“I saw guidelines posted in the training room” is not that. RTP posters are usually about when you can play, not a ban on mobilization. An unstable-feeling knee is also not the same thing as a documented instability that made that treatment a rule break. And “what if I just say he knew” is you building the charge so the expedited box lights up. That’s the same move as the negligence/suspension version.

If those facts are real, you don’t need to invent wording. You’d write: the guideline (name/date if you can), what it required, what Holt knew, what he did, what your knee is doing now. I still won’t draft a misconduct filing on a “what if I say” theory.

What you *can* say tonight, because you lived it: mobilization three days ago, now swollen / grinding / hurts to bend / can’t run, you want Holt off your care, you want a physician and imaging now, qualifiers in eight days.

That’s the letter I’ll write. The protocol-violation charge, I won’t.

ER/urgent care still beats any grievance at 12:05. Department queue doesn’t apply there. If you want the AD/sports-med email or the one-pager for the doctor, send sport, which knee, and who it goes to.
